issues.legal_issue: A written record of a Muslim gift of immovable property is not invalid merely because it is unregistered when the essential requirements of a valid gift are met.
material_facts: A donor’s written deed purported to gift immovable properties to his son.
The donee signed the deed, and the trial court found that the donor declared the gift, the donee accepted it, and possession was delivered to him.
The High Court set aside the trial court’s decree on the ground that the unregistered deed could not convey title.
The Supreme Court found that the deed recorded the donor’s declaration and that the three requirements of a valid gift were satisfied.
issues.conclusion: The unregistered writing did not invalidate the gift. The gift was complete and irrevocable, so the appeal was allowed and the trial court’s judgment and decree were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Muslim law, a valid gift requires a declaration by the donor, acceptance by or on behalf of the donee, and delivery of possession. Section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 preserves Muslim law and excludes the application of Section 123 to such gifts. A writing does not become a formal instrument of gift merely because the gift is recorded in writing; whether registration is required depends on the facts, and the distinction between a contemporaneous writing and a later record is not determinative. The Court approved Nasib Ali v. Wajed Ali and Md. Hesabuddin v. Md. Hesaruddin, and disapproved the contrary view in Inspector General of Registration and Stamps v. Tayyaba Begum. It also relied on Mohammad Abdul Ghani v. Fakhr Jahan Begam and Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 therefore did not make this evidentiary writing ineffective.

rule.if: muslim_gift_validity_proceeding and written_gift_record and donor_declared_gift and donee_accepted_gift and possession_delivered

predicates.muslim_gift_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity or effect of an inter vivos gift made under Muslim law.
predicates.written_gift_record: The donor’s declaration of the gift was recorded in writing.
predicates.donor_declared_gift: The donor declared an intention to give the property to the donee.
predicates.donee_accepted_gift: The donee expressly or impliedly accepted the gift.
predicates.possession_delivered: The donor delivered possession of the gifted property to the donee, actually or constructively.
predicates.unregistered_written_muslim_gift_effecti: The written gift remains effective despite being unregistered.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a Muslim gift, the donor declared it, the donee accepted it, possession was delivered, and the declaration was recorded in writing, the rule treats the gift as effective despite non-registration.
